title: Crestfall
objective: Walk the town. Learn where [missing person] went.

default: In the morning you can see how much of Crestfall is left.

The baker's is open, and Reisa, who was baking before you were born, is at work in it without a word to anyone. The church is open too, with the Ashen Covenant's flag above the door, which is new since your day. The smith's is shut, and so are the cooper's and the chandler's.
You walk down the main street counting the closed shops, as you counted the wrong things on the pier last night. It is a habit, and you cannot seem to stop it.

The fountain in the market square has been dry for months; you can tell by the stain on the stone where the water used to stand. Somebody has left a bunch of flowers at its foot. Nobody has cleared them away, and they have been there long enough to go quite grey.

default.text: Aldous didn't look up when you left this morning.

text.commander:
You walk through Crestfall as you would through any position you had been sent to hold.

It could be defended, but nobody has thought to. There is no proper patrol. The Compact has soldiers on one gate and has left the rest of the town unwatched. There are fewer people about than you remember, or else they are keeping indoors, which comes to the same thing. The Covenant is very much in evidence, and the Compact has a garrison. Nobody in authority seems to have noticed the Rootless camp at all, and you wonder whether that is carelessness or policy.
text.arcane:
You walk through Crestfall and look at it as you would look at any site, for what has built up there over the years.

If you let your eyes go a little out of focus you can see the curse, or rather what it is doing. Everything has a faint grey cast, and sounds come to you muffled, as though through a curtain. Reisa's bread very likely tastes as it always did. It is the pleasure in baking it that is going.

That is how the curse spreads. It does not kill anybody. It simply takes away their reasons for getting up.
text.ranger:
You walk through Crestfall and look it over as you would any ground.

There are no animals in the town at all. You find one cat, under a porch on the north side, and it looks at you as if it knows perfectly well it is the last cat in the street and has decided to stay anyway. You think the better of it for that.

From the market square you can see the tree line to the east. It is nearer than it used to be, not by much, perhaps twenty yards, but you can tell. The forest is taking ground, slowly.
text.cipher:
You walk through Crestfall and collect what you can.

There are five people on the main street before eight o'clock. Two are Compact soldiers with nothing much to do, one is a Covenant priest, and two are townspeople who walk briskly and do not stop to talk.

Everybody here knows everybody, so a stranger is noticed, and you are being noticed now. You make a point of seeing who is doing it.

choices.text: Go to the market square and see who is trading.

default.text: There are three stalls in the market. There used to be twelve. You counted them once as a child, one long afternoon, trying to work out which would give you something for nothing if you asked nicely.

choices.text: Find the Ashen Covenant shrine and see who they are.

default.text: The flag is new, but the building is not. It is the old alderman's hall, which the Covenant seems to have taken over. A priest is standing outside, though not, you think, waiting for anybody in particular.
You know the way without having to think about it. Your feet seem to remember before you do.

text.default:
There are three stalls in a square built for twelve, and the gaps between them are hard not to look at.

One sells grain, one cloth, and an old man has a stall of food that keeps: dried fish, smoked meat. The grain seller watches you come and seems to make up her mind about you, though you can't tell which way.

By now they trade with one another more than with the town. It is the market of a place that is getting ready for something and will not say so.
text.commander: The grain seller is the one in charge here. You can tell by the way the other two keep half an eye on her. She is the one to talk to.
text.arcane: The old man with the preserved food is watching you and making up his mind whether you are worth the trouble. You decide to speak to him.
text.ranger: The empty pitches tell you more than the stalls do. The ground is worn differently there, and people's feet still take them to where the stalls used to be.
text.cipher: You take the measure of all three in a glance. The grain seller is frightened but getting on with it. The cloth woman is going through the motions. The old man is watching you as though he knows something about you, or thinks he does.

choices.text: Go and talk to the grain seller.

success.text:
Her name is Hanna. She tells you about Crestfall briskly, like someone who has been answering the same questions for months.

It began three years ago in the villages to the east, she says, and has been creeping west ever since. Three families came in from Harrow, the village on the east road, six months back. They left because Harrow had emptied. Nobody was attacked. One by one everybody in Harrow lost the wish to stay, and walked east into the forest, and didn't come back.

"They don't come back," she says. "But they're not dead. Or nobody knows. Nobody's found anyone."

success_at_cost.text: She will talk, but carefully. The curse is spreading west, she says, and the villages to the east are mostly empty now. People come to Crestfall because it feels safer. "It probably isn't," she adds, and looks at once as if she wishes she hadn't.

failure.text: "Just selling grain today," she says pleasantly. She has done this before, you can tell. When a conversation looks like going somewhere awkward, she simply goes back to selling grain.

choices.text: Speak to the old man with the preserved food.

success.text:
His name is Corvin. He has lived in Crestfall for eighty years, and he knows things as old men in small towns do, because he was there when they happened.

He saw [missing person], and he tells you so straight out, which surprises you. "Asking about the ruins," he says. "Same as you're about to." He looks at you hard. "Went out to the camp in the end. The woman there, Maret, sent them east."

He hands you a piece of dried fish you didn't ask for and looks away, and you understand that he has finished.

success_at_cost.text: He has been watching you since you came into the square, and now he seems to decide to tell you a little. [missing person] was here, he says, and went out to the camp. He looks away before you can ask him anything more.

failure.text: He watches you and does not get up. If you want anything, he seems to say, you can come to him. He tells you his prices, and that is all you get today.

choices.text: Buy a sack of grain for the camp outside town.

default.text:
Hanna weighs it twice. When you tell her where it is going she takes a coin back off the pile and pushes it across to you.

"They had my brother's boy out there all winter," she says. "Tell them it's from the grain stall."

choices.text: Buy dried fish from the old man for the road.

default.text: He wraps four fish in paper without asking how many you want. "For the road," he says. "Everyone who buys fish from me these days is going east."

choices.text: Go to the town gate and see what the Compact soldiers want.

default.text: The soldier on the gate saw you leave the inn this morning. You rather think he has been waiting for you.

text.default:
Two things happen, one after the other, as you go through the market.

The first is that Hanna from the grain stall stops you and lowers her voice. "You were asking about the Rootless." She didn't hear you ask, you notice. She heard about it, which is quicker. "Maret, the woman who runs the camp. She's careful. Don't go out there offering her things. She doesn't want things from people like you. She wants to know why she should trust you."

The second is that an old woman you don't know presses a piece of bread into your hand. "The camp fed my daughter when the town wouldn't," she says. "Whatever they tell you about them, you remember that." She has walked off before you can ask her name.
text.commander:
That is twice in half a minute that people have told you things without being asked. In a frightened town people get generous when they see somebody trying to make sense of it. They want you to get it right.

You take it to mean that the Rootless have friends in the town, and that Maret is trusted, after a fashion. The camp helped people when helping was a risk, and people have not forgotten it.
text.arcane:
Two people, one after the other, very different from each other, have told you the same thing in different words: go carefully, and don't take anything for granted.

So far nobody in the town has said anything against the Rootless that was more than suspicion.
text.ranger:
Both women are easy enough to read. Hanna wants to help, and is a little afraid you will make things difficult. The old woman loves somebody the Rootless looked after, and there is no arguing with that.

You had better go to the camp.
text.cipher: Hanna's advice is practical and the old woman's is not, but between them they tell you more about Maret than either would alone. She is trusted by people who do not trust easily, and she has made herself necessary in a town that tried very hard to do without her.

default.text: You go east out of the market, past the last of the houses, along something that is not quite a path, and in among the first of the trees.

choices.text: Spend more time in town before you go to the camp.

default.text: You spend the rest of the morning going round the few shops that are still open and picking up what you can. In the afternoon you go out to the camp.

choices.text: Visit the Compact at the gate first.

default.text: The gate is five minutes' walk. Cael is on duty there, and he looks up as you come, so he has been watching for you.
The shrine is in the old alderman's hall, with a grey flag over the door. Somebody has swept the steps this morning.

default: You go left at the baker's and down the hill, past the old mill wall, which was falling down when you were a child and has fallen down a good deal more since. You turn the corner, and there it is.
It has a new door in the old frame. Somebody has painted the shutters a colour you would never have chosen, and the window boxes are full of plants you don't recognise.
Of course somebody lives there, and has for years. You went away and did not come back, and the house has gone on without you, as houses do.
You stand in the street in front of it longer than you mean to.

default.text: This is where [missing person] used to wait for you in the mornings, sitting on your step with their back to the door so your mother would not see them and send them home.
[missing person] used to wait for you at the corner by the mill wall, where your mother could not see from the window. The wall is lower now. You could see over it.
It was [missing person]'s house too. They had the room at the back, over the yard, and they kept it after you went. Somebody else's curtains hang in that window now.
[missing person] walked you home along this lane after your first long day of work, stopped at the corner, and told you that you would be good at it. Then they walked back the way they had come.
[missing person] raised you in that house. They planted the climbing rose by the door the year you were born. The rose is gone. There is a boot scraper where it was.
The corner by the mill wall is where you and [missing person] used to stop and talk until it got dark, and then a while after. You never once walked them home. They never asked.

text.commander:
You stand in front of the house you grew up in and make yourself take it all in: the new door, the painted shutters, the strangers who live there now and have made it their own. You stand there until it stops troubling you.

You left, eleven years went by, and the house carried on. You turn and go back to the main street.
text.arcane:
You stand in front of the house you grew up in, and find it is not what you expected. It does not hurt, exactly. It is only rather strange.

The residue on the building lies in layers. Your own is faint now, eleven years old, and the lives of other people lie over it. You look for your traces and find them where you would expect: at the window of your old room, in the corner of the yard where you used to sit, on the doorstep.

There is still a little of you in the place, as there is a little of everybody in the house they grew up in. It is smaller than you remember.
text.ranger:
You find yourself looking the house over before anything else, which you have caught yourself doing before. It is sound. The people who live there look after it. The yard at the back has been dug over for vegetables.

Then you let yourself feel it, for a moment. The person you came for grew up a few streets from here. That will do.
text.cipher:
You stand in front of the house you grew up in and allow yourself, just for a minute, not to be working.

The curtains and the door are somebody else's now. The shadow on the paving is exactly the shape it always was.

You have stayed too long. You turn and go back.

choices.text: Knock, and introduce yourself to whoever lives there now.

success.text:
A woman in her thirties opens the door. She is wary at first, and then, when you explain, quite friendly.

She was born in Crestfall and moved into the house with her husband six years ago, and she knew a few of the people who knew you. She asks you in for something hot, and you go.

Inside it has all been changed, and under the changes it is exactly the same. You sit in the kitchen with your cup and she tells you about the town. Then, without your asking, she says, "Somebody came here last year asking about you. Or somebody like you. They described the family who used to live here, and asked about the old ruins."

So [missing person] came here, to your old house, looking for something about you, or about where you came from.

success_at_cost.text:
She opens the door and is polite but reserved. You explain who you are. She nods, and tells you one useful thing: about fourteen months ago she saw [missing person] walking east on the road, alone, and in no doubt about where they were going.

"I remember thinking they knew where they were going," she says. "You don't see that much now. People here don't look as though they know where they're going."

failure.text:
A man opens the door. He doesn't know you, he has things to do, and he says so quite kindly and shuts the door.

You stand on the step a moment, and then you go.

choices.text: Don't knock. Look, and then go.

default.text: You stay just long enough to finish the thought, and go before it can turn into anything else.

text.default:
Somebody calls "[player]" across the street. It is the name people here knew you by, not the one you have used since. It comes from a man of about your own age, and it is a moment before you place him.

It is Goran. The two of you used to run the east field fence together in the summers, a job your families shared. You haven't thought of him in years.

He crosses over and shakes your hand. He is glad to see you, and a little afraid of what your coming back may mean.
text.commander:
Goran was always the sort of boy who would grow up to keep a place going by doing the jobs nobody notices until they stop being done. You can see he has had a great deal of that lately.

"It's good to see you," he says, and he means it. It is good, you suppose, to see somebody from before, who remembers what the town used to be.
text.arcane:
Goran looks at you with recognition and with a kind of relief. You have seen that look on people who have been frightened a long time and think they have met somebody who might understand.

"You're back," he says. "Are you here because of..." He stops. "You've heard what's been happening."
text.ranger:
You remember the east field, the long summers and the poor pay, and how the two of you could work all day without needing to talk. He has got heavier, his hair is going, and he is looking at you as though you might have an answer.

"Heard you were at the Tallow," he says. News travels quickly in a town this size.
text.cipher:
Goran knew you before you learned to be careful about who knew you. He is looking at you as though it were eleven years ago.

That may be useful. People tell old friends what they would never tell a stranger.

default.text:
He finds you a bench near the old fountain and tells you. It isn't everything, but it is more than anybody else has told you, and it comes out in a rush, as if he has been waiting for someone to tell.

It started two winters ago, he says, with the animals, and then the crops, and then people. Three families left Harrow and came here. The Compact came eight months ago, the Covenant took over the alderman's hall, and the Rootless set up their camp on the edge of the forest.

"Your person," he says suddenly. You haven't mentioned anybody. "The one you've come for. I saw them, fourteen months back or so. They spent a week asking questions and then went out to the camp." He looks at the trees to the east. "Then they went east, and nobody I know went to find out what happened to them."

choices.text: "Did you see [missing person] when they were here?"

default.text:
He is nodding before you have finished the name. "I saw them," he says. "We talked a few times. They were asking about the history of the place, the old city under the forest, the ruins. The things people here grow up not asking about."

He looks at his hands. "They didn't seem frightened. They seemed to have a purpose. I remember thinking either they knew something the rest of us didn't, or they were about to find out something they weren't expecting."

He looks at you. "I take it they never came back."

choices.text: Keep it short. You have things to do.

default.text:
You talk for a few minutes. It is friendly and it is not nearly enough, and you both know it. He tells you where he lives, the house with the blue door on the north lane, and says to come by if you need anything.

You may well need to. You go.
